4076e155934d5d211b12ad88300d040d44b12b3a.title: Banks of the Oise at Dawn
4076e155934d5d211b12ad88300d040d44b12b3a.genre_evidence: Banks of the Oise at Dawn Oil on canvas Louis Hayet was an important, early practitioner of Neo-Impressionism, or Pointillism, the practice of applying small strokes or dots of paint so that from a distance the hues visually blend together and create an intense sensation of color and light. Notice the way in which Hayet painted the pale dawn sky—and its reflection in the River Oise—with strokes of pink, orange, blue, yellow, and green paint. When seen at a distance, the effect is of early morning, before the sun has fully risen. ['France'] Painting

b47377f60ac6e28c0c18bfce301dd2ddf558d4be.title: The Red Kerchief
b47377f60ac6e28c0c18bfce301dd2ddf558d4be.genre_evidence: The Red Kerchief oil on fabric This painting depicts Monet's first wife, Camille, outside on a snowy day passing by the French doors of their home at Argenteuil. Her face is rendered in a radically bold Impressionist technique of mere daubs of paint quickly applied, just as the snow and trees are defined by broad, broken strokes of pure white and green. ['France'] Painting

e61d1fc979aa2b3039ce48878b796c6e03a6e2a5.title: Edge of the Woods Near L'Hermitage, Pontoise
e61d1fc979aa2b3039ce48878b796c6e03a6e2a5.genre_evidence: Edge of the Woods Near L'Hermitage, Pontoise oil on fabric Born to a French-Jewish family on St. Thomas island in the Caribbean, Pissarro painted this monumental landscape when he was desperately poor and struggling to sell his paintings. It depicts a man slumbering in the sun-dappled backwoods of the Hermitage, a rural village near Pontoise, where the artist had been living since 1872. Restricting his palette to pure hues, Pissarro applied brushstrokes in systematic diagonal patterns, producing an effect that he likened to knitting. This canvas was included in the fourth Impressionist exhibition of 1879. ['France'] Painting

53de9761bf50731c35e2ed3133e9feb0693d496c.title: The Brook
53de9761bf50731c35e2ed3133e9feb0693d496c.genre_evidence: The Brook oil on fabric Although Cezanne exhibited twice with the Impressionists, he rejected his friends’ goals of capturing the fleeting effects of light and atmosphere in their art. Instead, he sought to create balance among the forms and colors in his compositions. This painting depicts the valley of the Arc River that runs southeast of Cezanne’s home in Aix-en-Provence. Throughout the composition, he juxtaposed strokes of different hues, describing the leaves, branches, and the stream with color rather than drawing the outlines of forms. ['France, late 19th-early 20th Century'] Painting

1d780a95f1598ae6e25e67919b061dd4afc4d0e8.title: Study for a Decoration for the Salle des Fêtes of the Town Hall of Paris's 11th arrondissement
1d780a95f1598ae6e25e67919b061dd4afc4d0e8.genre_evidence: Study for a Decoration for the Salle des Fêtes of the Town Hall of Paris's 11th arrondissement watercolor with black chalk framing lines on beige wove paper An avid draftsman, Victor Prouvé was known for his role in the École de Nancy, a group of artists active in the art nouveau movement, which integrated fine and decorative arts. This drawing relates to Prouvé's design for a mural intended to decorate the community center in the town hall of Paris's 11th arrondissement. By creating sophisticated designs for a broad public in such spaces, the artist sought to forge a role for vanguard art in everyday life. ['France'] Drawing

1d09faa7566085b920c0c3d41290657715e34d3d.title: The Deluge
1d09faa7566085b920c0c3d41290657715e34d3d.artist: Charles Guilloux (French, 1866–1946); L'Estampe Originale (blindstamp lower right)
1d09faa7566085b920c0c3d41290657715e34d3d.genre_evidence: The Deluge color lithograph Guilloux’s The Deluge appeared in the famous L’Estampe Originale, a series of nine albums of original prints published in Paris between 1893 and 1895, representing the pinnacle of fin-de-siècle printmaking. The albums included numerous landscapes by masters of the genre, including Camille Pissarro, Charles Dulac, Henri Rivière, and Joseph Pennell (all in this exhibition). In The Deluge, drenched poplar trees are reflected in shimmering pools of water. Guilloux incorporated the aesthetic of Art Nouveau into his entirely original, stylized landscapes. ['France'] Print

b666d2392594a4292cb12e2f08ada3df2e19fc47.title: The Promenade (Landscape with Cypresses)
b666d2392594a4292cb12e2f08ada3df2e19fc47.genre_evidence: The Promenade (Landscape with Cypresses) color lithograph on chine collé In 1891, Henri Cross began painting in a pointillist style influenced by Georges Seurat and Paul Signac. He also left Paris and moved to the south of France, settling in Saint-Clair, a small village near Saint-Tropez. There, he concentrated on seascapes and scenes of peasants in harmony with nature. The sensuous silhouettes of cypresses and the swaying circle of figures by the water’s edge exemplify Cross’s decorative treatment of landscape, also recalling the Japanese color woodcuts and Art Nouveau designs that inspired other neo-Impressionists at the time. ['France'] Print

080abad448e544ca3d67ba00b4835c2e88709f8e.title: The Race Track (Death on a Pale Horse)
080abad448e544ca3d67ba00b4835c2e88709f8e.genre_evidence: The Race Track (Death on a Pale Horse) oil on canvas Ryder’s subject was inspired by a horse race that took place in New York during 1888. One of the artist’s friends wagered $500 on the race and then died by suicide after the horse lost. Medieval symbolism infuses the composition: death appears as a skeleton on horseback holding a scythe with which it cuts down the living, while a snake—a sign of temptation and evil—slithers in the foreground. An intense man, Ryder worked on the painting for several years and was deeply reluctant to part with it. ['United States'] Painting

bfb97340b75d66d8daf0843a58c9982c7dbdd849.title: Adam and Eve
bfb97340b75d66d8daf0843a58c9982c7dbdd849.genre_evidence: Adam and Eve engraving Albrecht Dürer’s iconic engraving was hugely impactful to the spread of natural symbolism in Europe. Drawing upon classical sculptural models, he represented Adam and Eve in perfect, uncorrupted beauty moments before tasting the forbidden fruit. The tree of knowledge, with its writhing serpent, is a fig tree, and the tree of life, which Adam clasps, is a mountain ash, native to Northern Europe. The elk, rabbit, cat, and ox are symbols of the four human temperaments—melancholic (gloomy), sanguine (sensual), choleric (cruel), and phlegmatic (slothful)—in perfect balance. But the cat and mouse hint at aggression to come, and the parrot, appearing like a beacon in the dark northern forest, heralds the promise of the Virgin Mary (the new Eve). ['Germany, early 16th Century'] Print

4a88cb5cdb52402afdd241b1218cd88ddc69b0bd.title: The Holy Family with Saint Elizabeth
4a88cb5cdb52402afdd241b1218cd88ddc69b0bd.genre_evidence:
The Holy Family with Saint Elizabeth engraving While this landscape might seem desolate and strange, it is rife with religious symbolism. The Virgin Mary and Christ on the right sit with Mary’s cousin, Saint Elizabeth, and her son, Saint John the Baptist. The Bible describes Elizabeth as past childbearing age; both she and Mary were granted virgin births by God. The barren trees, therefore, signify Elizabeth’s
infertility, while the fencelike enclosure denotes the enclosed garden of virginity. The trees also remind viewers of Eve’s sin in the Garden of Eden. Jacopo de’ Barbari placed lively grapevines on the dying trees, a metaphor for Christ. ['Italy'] Print

61bd8458495302e2a43deb1a1b72dcc2d53efd25.title: Midnight
61bd8458495302e2a43deb1a1b72dcc2d53efd25.genre_evidence: Midnight oil on fabric This painting depicts Abbeville, a city in northern France famous for its canals and architecture. It lies near the seaport of Boulogne-sur-Mer, Cazin's hometown and where he spent the last decades of his life painting the countryside, beaches, and nearby towns. Cazin specialized in landscapes, often influenced by his knowledge of English and Dutch painters. The title, Midnight, and the image itself suggest silence and stillness—Cazin's hallmarks—but only rarely did he attain this almost surrealistic atmosphere. Cazin was educated in Paris at the famous Ecole Gratuite de Dessins (Free School of Drawing), an innovative and unorthodox institution teaching drawing from memory. He studied there with fellow artists Henri Fantin-Latour (1836–1904), Auguste Rodin (1840–1917), and Alphonse Legros (1837–1911). They all shared an interest in Symbolism—the movement that sees symbols in reality and perceives reality through symbols. ['France'] Painting

95241980cc507773b23c878b1a3535052b2bc85d.title: Little Dance
95241980cc507773b23c878b1a3535052b2bc85d.genre_evidence: Little Dance collage With collages of densely interwoven scraps of paper gleaned from daily life, Schwitters produced dynamic compositions in which the interaction of the materials becomes a kind of dance. Notice here the way the color red "dances" among the subdued tones of white, gray, and ochre. ['Germany, 20th century'] Drawing

dfa234b6d7b4c88ed4d7c29b98aade697336ee59.title: Still Life
dfa234b6d7b4c88ed4d7c29b98aade697336ee59.genre_evidence: Still Life oil, sand, and mixed media collage on canvas The Spanish artist María Blanchard worked in Paris as a Cubist between 1916 and 1919. In Still Life, she portrayed multiple, simultaneous viewpoints in an abstract style based on geometry and flat planes. Although other Cubists used collage elements in their work, Blanchard was unique in her use of three-dimensional elements to create an image that fluctuates between the concrete and the illusionary. During her lifetime, Blanchard was celebrated by her fellow Cubists, and she shared studios with Juan Gris and Diego Riviera, the latter of whom described her as producing Cubism’s “finest works, apart from our master, Picasso.” ['France, Paris'] Painting

bd06ff98dd88ee6173f91726f093f5cbcbb5194d.title: Merz 3 Portfolio:  Plate 1
bd06ff98dd88ee6173f91726f093f5cbcbb5194d.genre_evidence: Merz 3 Portfolio:  Plate 1 lithograph Dada was a literary and art movement that began in Europe during World War I. It was characterized by cynicism, expressions of outrage at the conditions of the world, and rebellion against all established artistic conventions and traditional art forms. In 1919 Kurt Schwitters developed his own version of Dada named Merz which took the form of poetry, public recitals of nonsense, and collages. The verbal juxtapositions of unrelated words in his poems had a visual equivalent in compositions made up of bits of paper—urban debris that the artist avidly collected from the city streets. According to Schwitters, "Merz was the second syllable of Kommerz . . . it was cut out and glued on from an advertisement for the Kommerz und Privatbank (Commercial and Private Bank)." 5cc8c0d41c4b533f7706545174bbacb4a1b8fc50.title: Composition with Red, Yellow, and Blue
5cc8c0d41c4b533f7706545174bbacb4a1b8fc50.genre_evidence: Composition with Red, Yellow, and Blue oil on canvas During the 1910s, Piet Mondrian’s art progressed from Cubism to an increasingly abstract style based on the form of a grid. He completely abandoned the representation of natural appearances, limiting himself to horizontal and vertical rectangles and three primary colors (red, yellow, and blue) along with black and white. Intensely intellectual and deeply philosophical, Mondrian believed that following the devastation of World War I, such abstract compositions could contribute to a more harmonious society by communicating in a universal, visual language. ['Netherlands'] Painting
